articles.title: These South American Birds Can Match a Jackhammer's Ear-Splitting Volume, Making Them Some of the World's Loudest Known Avians

paras.en: From soft peeps to piercing calls, birds produce a wide range of sounds. But scientists recently discovered that two South American species take their calls to ear-splitting extremes, making deafening vocalizations on par with a jackhammer.

The bare-throated bellbird and the red-legged seriema can produce sounds at amplitudes that exceed 120 decibels, according to a study published September 29 in the journal Evolution. They’re now among the ranks of the white bellbird, another South American species, for the loudest known birds on the planet.

Researchers behind the new work didn’t specifically set out to find the world’s noisiest birds. Rather, they wanted to take advantage of recent technological advancements that have made it easier to measure vocal amplitude, the height of a sound wave and a key element of loudness.

“Until recently, it was very impractical to go out into the field and measure amplitude,” lead author João Menezes, an evolutionary biologist who conducted the research while at the University of Massachusetts Amherst, tells the New York Times’ Taylor Mitchell Brown. “It’s kind of stepping into a whole new world.”

The researchers started the project in Amherst, Massachusetts, during the Covid-19 lockdowns, when the unusually quiet circumstances made it easier to isolate and record bird song. They used a laser rangefinder to measure their distance from a specific bird, as well as a sound level meter, which allowed them to isolate that bird’s call from other noises.

“Even recording from my window or from the backyard, almost always that would be [the amplitude of] a new species,” Menezes tells the Washington Post’s Meghan Bartels. “It’s not often that you get to do this kind of exploratory science where you just go out into the field and document things for the first time, especially with birds.”

From Massachusetts, they headed next to Brazil, where they recorded birds in several different habitats. The scientists ultimately collected amplitude data on 123 bird species between December 2018 and January 2025, filling a major gap in scientists’ understanding of how loud birds can sing. Previously, scientists only had amplitude data for ten of those species—even the ubiquitous Canada goose had never been measured.

“We’ve been able to vastly increase the number of species for which there is amplitude data,” study co-author Jeffrey Podos, also an evolutionary biologist at the University of Massachusetts Amherst, says in a statement. “This is basic, foundational research that no one else has managed to do on this scale.”

Their amplitude database captures the impressive range of bird vocalization volumes. At the low end, they documented the dusky-throated hermit, a hummingbird that buzzes at a modest 64 decibels, about the same volume as a normal conversation. At the high end, the bare-throated bellbird and red-legged seriema are both about as loud as a trumpeting elephant or a chainsaw.

Comparing the amplitude data with the birds’ anatomy revealed that species with bigger bodies and wider mouth openings also tended to be the loudest. This is probably because “bigger birds have bulkier muscles, which are capable of creating greater internal pressures, which ultimately generate louder sounds, and then broader mouths allow more energy to radiate into the environment,” Menezes tells CNN’s Amarachi Orie.

Still, the researchers have many unanswered questions. The big one: Why are some birds so much louder than others? The researchers hypothesized that the loudest birds evolved their high-volume calls to attract numerous mates, or to communicate through dense vegetation. But those explanations don’t hold up for the red-legged seriema, so there must be some other factor driving the evolution of its loud vocalizations.

“The seriema is the opposite of those two things,” Menezes tells WBUR’s Barbara Moran. “It’s a super open-habitat bird, like pasture, and it’s strictly monogamous. So, it forms a pair for the breeding season, and that’s it.”

There’s no single answer to the question of which species holds the title of “world’s loudest bird”—it depends on how researchers define loudness. The bare-throated bellbird, for example, produced the loudest individual call, reaching nearly 131 decibels, per CNN. But when researchers averaged the loudest calls across individual birds, the red-legged seriema came out on top at nearly 121 decibels. Averaging the vocalizations’ peak volumes, on the other hand, allowed the white bellbird to take the lead at 127 decibels.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Scientists are still unraveling the evolutionary underpinnings of super loud birdsong. But in the meantime, their work could have important implications for conservation. For example, reliable amplitude data could help researchers use audio recordings to determine not just whether a species is present, but also how close those birds might be and how many individuals are nearby, Connor Wood, an ornithologist at Cornell University who wasn’t involved in the study, tells the Washington Post.
The findings could also help scientists better understand how birds may adapt to a changing world.

“Amplitude is so critical to the ability of birds to communicate with each other, that it is really important for us to understand exactly how that might be able to change,” Nathan Senner, an ornithologist at the University of Massachusetts Amherst who also wasn’t involved with the study, tells WBUR. “How they evolve is really fundamental to our understanding of how they might continue to evolve as our world changes.”

articles.title: A Community-Led Archaeology Dig on a Tiny Scottish Isle Has Unearthed a Medieval Monastery of 'International Importance'

paras.en: Historians have long known that Lismore, a small isle in the Inner Hebrides of Scotland, was home to a medieval monastery called Lios Mòr. Written records detail its sixth-century founding by St. Mo Luóc, one of the early monks who spread Christianity to northern Britain. But with very little archaeological evidence, apart from a broken granite cross, scholars could not confirm Lios Mòr’s size, style or significance—until now.

According to an article published in the journal Antiquity last week, a group of local volunteers led by archaeologist Clare Ellis, of the firm Argyll Archaeology, discovered an early medieval cemetery, various structures and “sophisticated craftworking of international importance” during excavations near Lismore’s 13th-century parish church.

“For centuries, Lismore’s early monastery was known mainly from written records and local tradition,” study co-author Gordon Noble, an archaeologist at the University of Aberdeen, says in a statement. “We can now see that it was a thriving center of worship, craftsmanship and learning, whose importance may have rivaled some of the best-known monasteries in early medieval Britain.”

Lismore’s historical society began searching for the site of Mo Luóc’s monastery in 2016. A “dynamic minority” of the island’s 170 or so residents crowdfunded and ran the digs, Robert Hay, a retired local scientist and dig participant, tells the Guardian’s Esther Addley. Grants, donations and yet more crowdfunding enabled the enthusiastic locals to hire Ellis to lead excavations near the site of Lismore’s 13th-century church, which still holds services.

“The research aimed to determine whether the site of the later medieval cathedral at Lismore was also the location of Mo Luóc’s early monastery, and to assess the scale, nature and status of the settlement,” Ellis says in the statement.

The dig uncovered a medieval cemetery containing at least six burials radiocarbon dated to between 650 and 1040 C.E. The archaeologists also unearthed a piece of an “early medieval cross slab,” per the study. In another area, they found more human remains and additional fragments of carved stone crosses.

“This was clearly a really important early Christian establishment,” Noble tells the Guardian. He compares it to Scotland’s famed Iona monastery, which was founded in 563 C.E. Both settlements were products of a medieval missionary movement that aimed to spread Christianity throughout pagan Britain. The monks succeeded. By the seventh century, Britain was Christianized.

Elsewhere on the cathedral property, researchers found the remains of an oval-shaped building paved with a layer of limestone. Dated to between the seventh and tenth centuries, it contained remnants of craftwork, handmade pottery, struck flint and an antler.

Another trench boasted extensive evidence of precious metalwork: more than 1,000 pieces of debris, including well-preserved molds and crucibles once used to melt down and cast gold, copper and silver. Hay describes them as “the best small crucibles ever found in Scotland,” per the Guardian.

Clay molds and crucibles are “unusual” finds for a monastic site, Noble tells Scientific American’s Jackie Flynn Mogensen. “It’s one of the largest metalworking assemblages we have from any site, secular or sacred, in this time period,” he adds.

The Lismore monastery appears to have an unusually large footprint. This, coupled with evidence of precious metals and craftsmanship, suggests the community was actually considerably wealthy and “far more than a small island church,” per the statement.
As Noble says to Scientific American, Lios Mòr appears to have been “a very significant mover and shaker” in its day. “It’ll be really exciting to see what shows up in the coming years.”

articles.title: September's Ozone Hole Was the Biggest It Has Been in 25 Years

paras.en: In September, the Antarctic ozone hole peaked at 10.6 million square miles—the second largest ever observed for this time of year.

Using data from the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service, scientists found that the ozone hole started growing earlier than usual in August. By September 20, it reached a size close to its October 2015 peak, when it was 10.8 million square miles.

To understand what’s happening, we first need to understand the ozone layer. The ozone layer lies in the Earth’s stratosphere and protects our planet from harmful ultraviolet (UV) radiation that can harm humans, plants and animals. The infamous ozone hole is actually a patch of depleted ozone in the stratosphere over Antarctica that is mainly caused by chemicals called chlorofluorocarbons, or CFCs. While the 1987 Montreal Protocol phased out the use of CFCs globally, they can persist in the atmosphere for decades.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The ozone hole’s size fluctuates every year. For about three months each fall—the Southern Hemisphere’s spring—the hole opens inside the stratospheric polar vortex, a large band of fast-spinning westerly winds that encircles Antarctica and the Southern Ocean. The vortex traps freezing air inside and leads to the formation of polar stratospheric clouds, writes a New Zealand-based research team in The Conversation. “Chemical reactions on particles in this rare type of cloud then activate ozone-depleting gases,” they add.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: This year brought a stronger and colder polar vortex. “We have unusually strong winds and cold temperatures over the pole that have created the conditions possible for the hole to grow to the size it has today,” research team member Hannah Kessenich, a physicist at the University of Otago in New Zealand, tells the Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC News). By late January, the hole will shrink again.
Did you know? Wildfires can destroy the ozone layer

- Climate change has increased the frequency of wildfires, which is not a good thing when it comes to mending the ozone layer. A study published in Nature in 2023 found that particles in wildfire smoke spark chemical reactions in the atmosphere that break down ozone.

So, should we be worried? “This year’s ozone hole shouldn’t be a cause for alarm,” Kessenich told Live Science's Sascha Pare in an email. “However, there are still many unanswered questions. It’s something we need to keep a close eye on.”

Kessenich and other experts underscore the fact that the ozone hole size we’re currently seeing isn’t a sign that the Montreal Protocol isn’t working. “We look at the depth of the hole rather than the area to assess how we’re coming along in terms of the recovery from those chemicals,” Kessenich says to ABC News.

In fact, this year’s hole isn’t as deep as it has been in previous years, and year-to-year variability is to be expected. “We have to look at the longer term trends, and those metrics continue to tell us that the ozone hole is slowly recovering as expected,” adds Susan Solomon, an atmospheric chemist at MIT, in an email to Live Science.

There will, however, be impacts on weather across the Southern Hemisphere. A larger ozone hole shifts the Southern Annular Mode into a positive phase, which affects winds and precipitation in different areas. In Australia, for example, it causes increased rainfall on the country’s southeast coast, Kessenich and her colleagues write in The Conversation.

Researchers are still trying to understand how climate change impacts the strength of the polar vortex, and why bigger ozone holes are persisting longer than they used to. It could be that changes in global atmospheric dynamics are making longer-lived ozone holes more likely, which in turn could mean our timelines for ozone recovery need to be adapted.
“It's too soon to tell what has been driving dynamical variability in recent years, but more research is needed,” Kessenich says to Live Science.

articles.title: AlterMe Review: Fitness Built Around My DNA
articles.author: Emily Peck

paras.en: When I was asked to review AlterMe’s fitness system that claims to use DNA and biometric data to create a personalized fitness, nutrition, and recovery program, I was intrigued. I’ve used some of the best fitness trackers before, but have never tried a system that combines DNA testing, personalized workouts, nutrition insight, and its own smart wearable all within a single ecosystem.

I’m someone who needs constant fitness motivation to stay on track. Rather than push myself through strenuous weights and cardio, I prefer feel-good Pilates and an ice bath at my local David Lloyd gym. But in an effort to step out of my comfort zone and try something a little more challenging, I decided to give AlterMe a go.

I’ve used numerous fitness apps over the years, such as Bala and Freeletics, but not one that suggests specific fitness workouts based on my DNA testing results. AlterMe combines guidance across exercise, nutrition, sleep, and recovery, going beyond simply reporting on your DNA and biometric data to suggest small, manageable actions to drive behavioral change over time.

articles.title: Feds Got Warrants to Use Fake Cell Towers to Hunt Down Don Lemon’s Producer
articles.author: Dhruv Mehrotra

paras.en: US law enforcement agents obtained authorization to use a controversial surveillance device capable of intercepting cell phone signals to find and arrest a 21-year-old college student who helped produce journalist Don Lemon’s coverage of an anti-ICE protest, court filings show.

The former student, Jerome Richardson, who has since graduated from Temple University, is among 39 people charged with conspiring to violate worshippers’ civil rights and interfering with religious worship at Cities Church in St. Paul, Minnesota, in January. Protesters said they targeted the church’s January 18 service because one of its pastors, David Easterwood, also led ICE’s St. Paul field office. Those charged include journalists Georgia Fort and Lemon, a former CNN host, who say they were there to cover the demonstration.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Twelve days after the protest, judges in two states began signing warrants authorizing agents to use so-called cell-site simulators, commonly known as Stingrays or IMSI catchers, to target Richardson’s phone: one in Minnesota on January 30 and another in Pennsylvania the next day. The purpose, his lawyers wrote in a motion seeking to exclude the tracking evidence, was “locating and arresting him.”

Agents also applied for cell-site simulator warrants targeting the phones of Fort and Jamael Lundy, then a Minnesota State Senate candidate. They separately sought pen register orders, which can log the numbers a phone contacts, for Fort and a number WIRED traced to Lemon. It's unclear whether a judge approved any of those applications.

The records reviewed by WIRED do not establish whether investigators actually deployed a cell-site simulator to locate Richardson or whether judges approved the applications targeting Fort and Lundy. In a July letter filed in court, Fort’s lawyers said prosecutors “did not know” whether the surveillance applications had been authorized or had yielded evidence.

Cell-site simulators impersonate cell phone towers to locate a target’s phone. In doing so, they can also collect identifying information from any nearby cellular device, including those belonging to people who aren’t suspected of a crime. That indiscriminate collection has made the devices controversial among privacy advocates, who describe them as dragnet surveillance tools.

The use of cell-site simulators has long been shrouded in secrecy. FBI records released in 2023 showed that police borrowing its simulators had to agree to keep details of their use secret, even in court. Privacy advocates have long warned that the devices could be turned against protesters and journalists.

“Using an advanced surveillance capability such as a cell-site simulator against members of the free press for reporting stories that are unfavorable to the president is an appalling attack on the First Amendment,” says Cooper Quintin, senior staff technologist at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, a tech-focused civil liberties nonprofit. Quintin has spent years researching the devices and developing tools to help people detect them. Using EFF’s detection software, WIRED found evidence suggesting a cell-site simulator was deployed near the 2024 Democratic National Convention in Chicago, though who operated it and for what purpose remain unknown.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Attorneys for Lemon, Lundy, and Fort did not respond to requests for comment. Richardson’s attorneys declined to comment on the record.

The previously unreported warrants are a product of a campaign of contentious investigative tactics waged by federal agents in pursuit of people connected to the protest at Cities Church. According to court records, the Department of Homeland Security demanded journalists’ telephone and YouTube records under a customs authority that requires no prior judicial approval. Agents also sought records identifying everyone who had purchased a particular beanie at REI in the Minneapolis–St. Paul area over a period of more than two years. Defense attorneys have identified 92 customs summonses and are challenging the government’s authority to issue them.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The cell-site simulator warrants raise serious questions about both the accuracy of the information investigators presented to judges in their effort to obtain authorization for surveillance tool’s use, as well as why they sought such intrusive tracking to find Richardson in the first place.

The affidavits supporting the applications to track Richardson claimed video showed Fort, Lemon, Richardson, and others “chanting with agitators.” Prosecutors have since conceded that Lemon and Fort did not chant. According to her lawyers, the government acknowledged that the false claim appeared in at least 15 warrant affidavits.

DHS policy says cell-site simulators are deployed only “in the fraction of cases in which the capability is best suited to achieve specific public safety objectives,” but it’s unclear what specific public safety reason justified its use in this case. Investigators obtained a second simulator warrant to locate Richardson, then a senior at Temple University, two days before he walked up to a federal courthouse in Philadelphia and voluntarily surrendered. He was released on bond that afternoon.

The Justice Department responded to WIRED’s request for comment by writing in an email that the department “speaks through its court filings.” DHS declined to discuss ongoing investigations or investigative methods and referred questions to the US Attorney’s Office for the District of Minnesota, which did not respond to a request for comment.

The warrant was signed January 31, the same day Richardson posted a YouTube video saying he expected to enter federal custody “in the coming days,” suggesting he had no intention of fleeing. It is unclear whether the warrant preceded the video, leaving questions about why investigators sought such an intrusive tool to find someone who was publicly anticipating his arrest and whom prosecutors agreed to release the day he surrendered.
While Richardson’s suppression motion asks to suppress evidence obtained from the phone tracking, it does not specify whether agents used a simulator or obtained evidence through either.

A former federal prosecutor who spent a decade working on counterterrorism cases says using a simulator to locate someone is not necessarily unusual. But based on the court records they reviewed about Richardson’s case, they called the government's tactics aggressive: “I don’t understand why it would be at all necessary.” They spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak on the record

Richardson, a St. Paul native, had led an NAACP chapter at 16 and served as executive director of Minnesota Teen Activists, according to his fundraiser’s organizer. He described his work for Lemon as handling logistics and connecting him with local contacts. He drove the journalist to Cities Church, where Lemon livestreamed the demonstration and interviewed protesters and churchgoers. Prosecutors allege Richardson joined chants and obstructed congregants.
In his video, Richardson defended his role. “I was proud to support his work,” he said of Lemon. “This is the price of being unapologetic about humanity and love of Christ.”

The government’s initial effort to obtain arrest warrants met resistance from judges. A magistrate judge refused five of eight warrants, and after an appeals court rejected the Justice Department's bid to override that decision, the department withdrew its request. In a filing with the appeals court, the chief judge wrote that two of the five “were not protestors at all; instead, they were a journalist and his producer” and that there was “no evidence that those two engaged in any criminal behavior.” Prosecutors later secured a grand jury indictment on January 29.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The way the government chose to arrest some defendants has also drawn objections from defense lawyers. Lemon’s attorneys say in court filings that prosecutors rejected their offer to arrange his surrender; agents instead arrested him shortly before midnight at a Beverly Hills hotel while he was covering the Grammy Awards. Fort’s lawyers say agents arrested her at home rather than allowing her to turn herself in.

articles.title: How Apple Puts Indigenous Languages on the iPhone Keyboard
articles.author: Julian Chokkattu

paras.en: Chuck Hoskin Jr. fondly recalls watching a room full of Cherokee immersion students crowd around a screen to watch How to Train Your Dragon. Except Hiccup and Astrid weren't speaking English—the protagonists were speaking Cherokee, dubbed by voices from the local community.

“They're hearing it in our mother tongue—that didn't happen a generation ago,” Hoskin Jr., principal chief of the Cherokee Nation, tells WIRED. “We're a long way, thankfully, from rote classroom instruction and memorization to a world where kids can see the sort of creativity that sparks imagination and helps every kid become more articulate and literate.”

The Cherokee Nation has around 1,500 active speakers left, and most are over 70. Hoskin Jr. says the community is rapidly losing that generation, which is why it has spent time training up second-language learners. It even has a baby immersion program, hoping their first words are Cherokee.

“The foes we’ve had historically are the so-called Age of Discovery, colonization, the displacement of our people economically and geographically, boarding schools,” he says. “But it's nothing compared to the mathematics we’re up against now. Which is why we’re filled with this urgency every day to do all we can to find partners that can help us accelerate what we want to do.”

One of those accelerants is Apple. The Cherokee Nation has long collaborated with the iPhone maker, and Cherokee was the first Native American language included in iOS in 2010. Today, Apple says its iOS keyboard supports more than 200 languages and language variants, with a handful added last year in iOS 26, like Haitian Creole and Nez Perce. In iOS 27, it expanded support for Indigenous languages to include other Native American languages like Blackfoot, Comanche, and Northern East Cree.

The goal is to meet young people where they already spend much of their waking hours: phone screens. Hoskin Jr. says that to revitalize and save a language, it has to become accessible. Apple says the effort isn't as simple as translating words. It’s a multi-year endeavor that requires deep research, and the company leans on community members for their expertise.

But the process doesn’t start in Cupertino. It actually begins with Unicode. You may have heard of the name—it’s the organization that approves and standardizes the new emoji that appear on your smartphone every year. It also handles time zone localization, currency names, imperial versus metric, and so on.

Before you can type or read a character on a smartphone screen, it needs to exist as a recognized character in the Unicode Standard. “Everything does start with Unicode in terms of a language, but it actually starts with characters and scripts,” says Unicode CEO Toral Cowieson. “We now have more than 157,000 characters that are included.”

Cowieson calls Unicode a kind of digital Switzerland—a neutral consortium where rivals like Apple, Microsoft, and Google sit at the same table as linguists and volunteer contributors. (Cowieson told WIRED earlier this year that Unicode had only four full-time employees.) Proposing a language, verifying it, and then encoding the character set can take three to five years.

After a script is encoded, platforms like Apple and Google need to add font support. Without this step, a character could appear as an empty box—often called “tofu.” Next is orthography: a set of rules and systems for writing a language. Often, languages have a well-defined orthography, but when it’s not standardized, communities use ad hoc replacements because historically available keyboards don't support it.

Take the glottal stop—the speech sound made in the throat between the syllables when you say, “uh-oh.” Some languages have distinct characters for glottal stops, but as some keyboards don’t support them, many indigenous cultures use alternatives, like a question mark, to represent the sound. That's when Apple connects with the community to figure out the best way to represent the sounds in digital text.

That brings us to the keyboard layout. When a community already has an established physical keyboard layout—like Osage—Apple adapts it directly to the software keyboard. Some cultures prefer the QWERTY layouts people are already familiar with.

Other languages need more custom approaches. For example, Nez Perce, or Nimipuutímt, does not use capital letters. Rather than having the Shift key toggle traditional uppercase letters, Apple repurposed it to reveal an accented secondary layer, so users don’t have to hold down individual keys to see those characters, which can slow typing. In the Cherokee language, each character mostly represents a consonant combined with a vowel sound, a form known as syllabary. Apple added adaptive vowel keys on the bottom row, so when a user types a consonant, these keys change to show the vowel combinations they can make.

paras.en: That’s a newer change to the Cherokee keyboard—one Apple approached the community about, meaning building a keyboard for a language isn’t a one-and-done project.

But digitizing an indigenous culture’s language hasn't always been harmless. Genner Llanes-Ortiz, a Maya scholar and researcher at Bishop's University, studies how Indigenous people use digital technologies to reclaim language heritage. He recalls how Māori speakers rejected proposals to sell their language to tech companies.

“There’s a historical memory about the ways of dispossession that Indigenous peoples have experienced in the world,” Llanes-Ortiz says. “Māori working in their own revitalization efforts have been very firm in protecting access and storage of their linguistic materials because they have been exploited. They have experienced extraction of knowledge in the past.”

Language sovereignty and data ownership are top of mind, according to Chirasree Mandal, an Apple software engineer. “We don’t own anything, and we make it very clear that we are not trying to silo any data that we gain from this process,” she says. “It’s about making sure that the best choice for representing someone’s language is being made on our platform so they feel good using it.”

For its part, a Google spokesperson tells WIRED it has a long history of bringing lesser-known and Indigenous languages to its platforms so people can communicate, pointing to collaborations to integrate languages like Manx and Māori. Google also says it’s exploring how generative AI can simplify the coding and research required for new languages, but “successful integrations require direct participation from native speakers” for the keyboard to meet the community’s needs.

Hoskin Jr. says that writing in syllabary is seen as a badge of honor for young Cherokee speakers. People type their names in Cherokee on Facebook—that’s empowering. But he sees that progress as vulnerable to broader political rhetoric in the US that pushes a monolithic, English-speaking America, which he says bypasses several chapters, including Native American history.

“The greatest enemy we have right now for saving the Cherokee language is the passage of time and the fragility of human life,” Hoskin Jr. says. “Time is precious to everyone, but particularly precious to us in this mission.”

articles.title: NFL suspends 49ers' Dre Greenlaw for unsportsmanlike conduct

paras.en: Oct. 12 (UPI) -- The NFL suspended San Francisco 49ers linebacker Dre Greenlaw for one game for unsportsmanlike conduct in Week 5, the league announced Monday.
Greenlaw's suspension stems from an incident that occurred in the second quarter of the 49ers' 32-29 win over the Seattle Seahawks on Sunday in Seattle.
A source told NFL Network that Greenlaw plans to appeal the suspension.
The veteran linebacker performed a headbutt -- while wearing his helmet -- on Seahawks linebacker Ernest Jones IV, who was not wearing his helmet, on the Seattle sideline Sunday at Lumen Field.
Greenlaw drew a personal foul and was ejected for the incident, which occurred after he delivered a late hit on Seahawks quarterback Sam Darnold.
Greenlaw totaled three combined tackles against the Seahawks. He logged 37 combined tackles and a forced fumble through his first five starts of 2026.
He is not eligible to return until Oct. 20. The 49ers will host the Washington Commanders on Oct. 19 in Santa Clara, Calif.

articles.title: European Union forms new support mission for Lebanon

paras.en: BEIRUT, Lebanon, Oct. 12 (UPI) -- The European Union decided Monday to establish a new support mission to advise and strengthen the Lebanese Army and internal security forces for an initial period of three years.
EU Foreign Affaires Ministers agreed to launch a new European Union Support Mission in Lebanon, or EUSM Lebanon, during a meeting in Brussels, according to an EU statement.

Kaja Kallas, high representative for foreign affairs and security policy, said the mission will advise and assist the Lebanese Armed Forces and Internal Security Forces to "strengthen territorial control, border security and internal security."

"Europe is invested in Lebanon's future," Kallas said, adding that with this new mission, the EU continues to support the country's institutions in "restoring full sovereignty and building lasting stability for the Lebanese people."
According to the Council of the EU, the mission will have an initial three-year mandate and comprise military and civilian pillars.

The military pillar will provide advisory support and training to strengthen the Lebanese Army's capabilities in "border security and maritime security," including intelligence, surveillance and counter-smuggling.

The civilian pillar will support the Internal Security Forces through "advisory support and specialized training" in areas such as cybercrime and anti-smuggling, as well as efforts to strengthen port security governance, including at the Port of Beirut.

Lebanese President Joseph Aoun welcomed the EU's decision to support the country's military and security institutions, saying it reflects "Europe's firm commitment to Lebanon's security and stability."

In a statement, Aoun said the EU's new mission would help strengthen the capabilities of Lebanon's legitimate institutions, extend the state's authority across its entire territory, and secure its borders, in line with the government's decisions on restricting weapons to legitimate security forces.

The EU decision comes as Lebanon seeks to strengthen state control over its territory and disarm Hezbollah, while the mandate of the United Nations peacekeeping force in southern Lebanon, or UNIIFIL, is to expire at the end of this year.

articles.title: 'Breaking Bad' actor R.J. Mitte dies at 34

paras.en: Oct. 12 (UPI) -- Actor R.J. Mitte has died at 34 in Brownsville, Texas, his representatives confirmed Monday with Deadline and The Hollywood Reporter. They did not give a cause of death.
"It is with profound sadness that we share the tragic passing of beloved actor, philanthropist and passionate disability rights advocate R.J. Mitte," the representatives said in a statement.
Most famously, Mitte played Walter White Jr. on Breaking Bad. In the AMC drama, Walter White Sr. (Bryan Cranston) became a crystal meth dealer to pay bills after he was diagnosed with cancer.

Both Mitte and his character on the show had cerebral palsy. Mitte was an ambassador for United Cerebral Palsy and is listed on the board of directors of his family's organization, The Mitte Foundation.

Following Breaking Bad, Mitte appeared on episodes of Switched at Birth and Now Apocalypse and the movies Triumph and Love Me Dead, as well as in other projects. His film Talking to Strangers premiered in July.

articles.title: Kacey Musgraves Is Dogging Kristi Noem After Trump Appointee Says She’d Take Ella Langley Over Kacey ‘Any Day’
articles.author: Alicia Urrea

paras.en: Kacey Musgraves isn’t letting her critics get the last word.

On Monday (Oct. 12), the country star fired back at Kristi Noem, the former Homeland Security secretary and current U.S. special envoy, after Noem took a swipe at Musgraves for welcoming Texas Senate candidate James Talarico to one of her concerts over the weekend.
“I don’t think you have a dog in this fight but if you did you would have shot it,” Musgraves wrote on X, delivering a pointed jab at Noem’s controversial account of killing her family dog.

The exchange happened after Talarico attended Musgraves’ Middle of Nowhere Tour stop in Dallas on Saturday. The Democratic candidate shared a photo with the singer on social media, writing, “Thank you for having me last night, Kacey Musgraves!”
Noem subsequently shared a screenshot of Talarico’s post, using the moment to voice her preference for both another country star and Talarico’s Republican opponent in the Senate race.
“I’ll take [Ella Langley] over Kacey Musgraves any day,” Noem wrote. “And if I’m choosin’ Texas, I’ll take Ken Paxton over James Talarico.”

The reference to “Choosin’ Texas” was a nod to Langley’s country hit, which spent 24 weeks at No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 before Taylor Swift‘s “Patient Zero” ended its historic run this month. The song’s unprecedented chart success has helped make Langley one of country music’s biggest breakout stars of the entire year.

Musgraves’ response turned the former government official’s criticism into a reference to one of the most controversial stories from Noem’s political career. In her 2024 memoir No Going Back, Noem recounted shooting and killing her 14-month-old dog, Cricket, whom she described as having an aggressive temperament. The revelation drew widespread backlash following the book’s publication.
The incident therefore provided Musgraves the punchline to her response to Noem’s unsolicited comparison of the two country singers.
Neither Langley nor Paxton was directly involved in the social media exchange between Musgraves and Noem.

Both country singers have made their mark on the Billboard charts. Musgraves released her sixth studio album, Middle of Nowhere, on May 1, while Langley’s sophomore album, Dandelion, arrived in April. Langley’s “Choosin’ Texas” made history with its record-breaking Hot 100 run, while Musgraves continued her chart presence with new music from her latest album, with the project landing at No. 3 on the Billboard 200.

Musgraves has previously used her platform to speak out on political and social issues. Earlier this year, she invited The Mariachi Brothers to open several of her performances in Texas. The group had previously been detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement before being released in March, according to the Houston Chronicle.

articles.title: BTS & BIGBANG Lead Nominations for 2026 MAMA Awards: Full List
articles.author: Paul Grein

paras.en: BTS received five nominations for the 2026 MAMA Awards, which were announced on Monday (Oct. 12), the same day that first-round voting began for the 2027 Grammy Awards, which, for the first time, contains a dedicated Asian pop category, best Asian pop music performance.

BTS is nominated for artist of the year at the MAMA Awards,as well as best male group, album of the year for ARIRANG, best vocal performance group for “SWIM” and best music video for “2.0.” In addition, group member J-Hope received two nods for his feature on LE SSERAFIM’s “SPAGHETTI,” nominated in both best collaboration and best dance performance female group.

Another leading K-pop group, BIGBANG, received four nominations plus four more for solo projects by group members Taeyang and G-Dragon. BIGBANG is up for artist of the year and best male group, plus best music video and best dance performance male group for “BiiiG.” Taeyang received three nods as a soloist: artist of the year, best male artist and best dance performance male solo for his single “LIVE FAST DIE SLOW.” G-Dragon earned a nod with his feature on aespa’s “WDA (Whole Different Animal)” in the best collaboration category. G-Dragon won artist of the year at the 2025 ceremony.

articles.title: Metallica’s James Hetfield Has a Message for Entertainers Who Bring Their ‘Bullsh–‘ Agenda to the Stage
articles.author: Alicia Urrea

paras.en: James Hetfield doesn’t seem very interested in turning a Metallica concert into a political lecture.

During the band’s Las Vegas Sphere residency, the heavy metal frontman took a second to thank fans for traveling to see the group before making one thing clear: Metallica isn’t there to push an agenda.

“Unless you live in Vegas, you’ve come a long way to spend some time with Metallica,” Hetfield told the audience during the band’s Oct. 10 show. “And I just gotta say: Metallica is not here, like some other entertainers, to influence you with their bullsh–.”
Instead, the singer and guitarist said the band wants fans to leave their outside worries at the door.
“We are here to forget about all the outside sh–,” he continued. “Metallica’s agenda is love, energy and heavy music, baby!”

Hetfield didn’t name any specific entertainers he had in mind, leaving his comments open to interpretation. Still, his message was unmistakable: When fans show up for Metallica, he wants the music to take center stage.

And the band’s staying power speaks for itself. Metallica’s ReLoad returned to the Billboard charts following an expanded reissue, landing at No. 1 on the Top Hard Rock Albums chart. The achievement was the band’s sixth leader on the ranking, following the success of its 2023 album 72 Seasons.

The remarks came during Metallica’s Life Burns Faster residency at Sphere, the immersive Las Vegas venue that has become known for its enormous wraparound screen and elaborate visual productions. The band kicked off the run in October, becoming the first heavy metal act to headline the venue. The residency features a series of performances scheduled through March 2027.

While Metallica doesn’t want to get political onstage, that doesn’t mean the band has refrained from being outspoken throughout their decades-long career. Over the years, they’ve addressed subjects ranging from war and addiction to social alienation in their music and they were on the frontlines of the fight against Napster, becoming the first musicians to sue the controversial music-sharing service in 2000.

articles.title: Former ‘SNL’ Star Ego Nwodim Reacts to Shane Gillis’ Controversial Joke About Women
articles.author: Carly Thomas

paras.en: Ego Nwodim had a sassy reaction to Shane Gillis following his controversial monologue on Saturday Night Live.
After hosting the NBC sketch comedy program on Saturday, the comedian drew heat over his joke about women working out.

“I haven’t been to the gym in so long, I didn’t know women just dress like whores now,” Gillis said to the live audience. “Look, I’m sorry, there’s no other way to describe [it]. Have you seen it? I’ve seen it. The shorts? Have you seen the shorts? They’re neon, like, artificial bait-colored? And the wrinkles go around the cheeks and all combine at the butthole. And don’t look. You’re not allowed to look. For real, don’t look, because they are filming. I’m in the background of like 10 TikToks right now.”
