articles.title: Scientists discover why a 100-year-old mushroom disease won't go away

paras.en: Scientists discover why a 100-year-old mushroom disease won't go away

- Scientists have uncovered a surprising secret behind a mushroom disease that has frustrated growers for more than a century: It involves more than 17 species of harmful bacteria, not just one. The discovery could explain why treatments have struggled to stop the disease and open the door to more effective, eco-friendly solutions.

A disease that has troubled white button mushroom growers for more than 100 years is far more complicated than scientists previously believed. Researchers at the University of Florida have discovered that the problem involves a surprisingly diverse collection of harmful bacteria, rather than a single pathogen. The finding could help explain why the disease has been so difficult to control and lead to more effective ways to protect mushroom crops.
The discovery comes from a University of Florida study investigating bacterial blotch, a persistent disease that damages white button mushrooms and causes significant financial losses for growers.

White button mushrooms are a valuable specialty crop and a familiar ingredient in everything from salads and appetizers to everyday meals. Rich in nutrients and valued for their versatility, they are often promoted as an example of the "food is medicine" concept, which emphasizes the role of nutritious foods in supporting good health. Their nutritional benefits make them an important part of many healthy diets.
Despite their popularity, these mushrooms face a longstanding problem that can make entire portions of a harvest difficult or impossible to sell.
A Century-Old Mushroom Disease With Hidden Culprits

Bacterial blotch causes brown or yellow discoloration on mushroom surfaces, damaging their appearance and reducing their commercial value. The disease can also lower crop yields and shorten shelf life, making it a costly challenge for mushroom farms across the United States.

Adding to the difficulty, visible symptoms sometimes develop only after mushrooms have been shipped to grocery stores or purchased by consumers. This delayed appearance makes the disease especially troublesome for growers trying to ensure consistent product quality.

For many years, scientists primarily associated bacterial blotch with a single disease-causing bacterial pathogen. However, researchers at the University of Florida Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences (UF/IFAS) have now found that the disease involves a much more complex collection of pathogenic bacteria.

These microorganisms can thrive in the carefully controlled, humid indoor environments used for commercial mushroom cultivation. Because several bacterial species may contribute to the same disease, methods designed to target a single pathogen may not be sufficient.

"For years, the industry has struggled with treatments that provide inconsistent results against bacterial blotch," said Samuel Martins, co-author and assistant professor in the UF/IFAS Department of Plant Pathology. "As part of a separate $7 million U.S. Department of Agriculture grant involving Penn State, University of Delaware and UF/IFAS, we are developing advanced diagnostics and sustainable solutions to strengthen mushroom farms nationwide."
DNA Analysis Reveals More Than 17 Bacterial Species
To investigate what was causing the disease, the research team collected affected mushrooms from several production facilities across the southern United States.

The scientists combined DNA sequencing, chemical profiling and conventional laboratory testing to identify the bacteria associated with the damaged mushrooms. DNA sequencing allowed them to examine the genetic identities of microorganisms present in the samples, while the additional tests helped characterize the bacteria and their disease-causing potential.
The results revealed a far more diverse group of pathogens than expected.

"We found more than 17 different species of pathogenic bacteria associated with the disease," said Sameerika Mudiyanselage, the study's lead author and a doctoral student of Martins and Romina Gazis at UF/IFAS Tropical Research and Education Center. "While two well-known bacterial pathogens dominated the known disease profile, we also detected a surprisingly high level of another group of bacteria that has not previously been linked to the mushroom disease."

The discovery suggests that scientists have been overlooking important contributors to bacterial blotch. Although two established pathogens remained prominent, the presence of additional bacterial groups indicates that the disease cannot be fully understood by studying those organisms alone.

This complexity may help explain why bacterial blotch has persisted for generations despite efforts to manage it. When several different microorganisms are associated with a disease, identifying the responsible bacteria, predicting outbreaks, and developing consistently effective treatments become more challenging.
The findings also suggest that growers may need more comprehensive detection methods capable of identifying a broader range of bacterial threats.

"We hope that expanding our research will lead to the development of better diagnostics and more effective treatments to address the full group of disease-causing bacteria in white button mushrooms," she said.
Natural Treatments Could Help Protect Mushroom Farms
The University of Florida researchers are now building on their findings with a follow-up study focused on more sustainable ways to manage bacterial blotch.
One promising approach involves testing plant-based essential oils, beneficial microorganisms, and other biological products as possible alternatives to conventional chemical treatments.

Essential oils contain naturally occurring compounds produced by plants, some of which have antimicrobial properties. Beneficial microbes may also help suppress harmful bacteria or make it more difficult for disease-causing organisms to thrive.

These approaches could eventually offer mushroom growers additional tools for controlling bacterial blotch while reducing their reliance on conventional chemical treatments. However, further research is needed to determine how well the potential alternatives work under real growing conditions.

"Ultimately, our goal is to provide growers with practical, science-based solutions that help strengthen mushroom farming systems," said Martins. "By understanding the complexity of bacterial blotch and the role of microbial communities, we can develop better eco-friendly management practices that reduce losses while improving sustainability."

The research changes the understanding of a disease that has affected white button mushroom production for more than a century. Rather than being the work of a single bacterial pathogen, bacterial blotch involves a diverse group of potentially harmful microorganisms, including previously overlooked species.

By uncovering this hidden complexity, scientists hope to improve disease detection, develop more reliable treatments, and reduce the crop losses that have long burdened mushroom producers. The findings could ultimately help make mushroom farming more resilient, productive and environmentally sustainable.
Materials provided by University of Florida. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

- Sameerika D. Mudiyanselage, Michelle Lee, Jose C. Huguet-Tapia, Romina Gazis, Samuel J. Martins. Genomic insights into a multispecies bacterial pathogen complex driving bacterial blotch in white button mushrooms. Microbiological Research, 2026; 309: 128532 DOI: 10.1016/j.micres.2026.128532

articles.title: What caused a mysterious atmospheric explosion in Siberia in 1908?
articles.author: Micah Hanks

paras.en: Fire erupted in the morning skies over Siberia on June 30, 1908, as an atmospheric explosion occurred that remains unmatched by any similar event in modern history.

That day, at approximately 7:15 a.m. local time, observers in Siberia's remote Tunguska region became witnesses to the entry of a brilliant fireball into Earth's atmosphere, trailing smoke across the dawn sky and culminating in a flash brighter than the sun itself. Within seconds, the explosion and resulting shock waves that followed reportedly knocked some members of the nearby Indigenous Evenki population off their feet, and caused damage to dwellings and livestock, while seismic instruments hundreds of miles away logged tremors caused by the blast.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The blast produced enough energy to flatten a significant stretch of the Siberian wilderness, marking an event that still serves as a cautionary tale — and a major point of reference — for modern planetary defense efforts. Yet some questions remain about exactly what happened, and what the implications are for future potential Tunguska-scale events. For many years after the events of that day, the cause of the blast — known today as the Tunguska event — remained unknown. With time, a likely culprit emerged: scientists now believe a small asteroid, estimated to have been just 130 feet (40 meters) in diameter, exploded after entering Earth's atmosphere.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Remarkably, scientists wouldn't get a firsthand look at the destruction caused by the Tunguska blast for almost two decades, due primarily to the extreme remoteness of the blast location. Further complicating scientific investigations were the First World War, the Russian Revolution, and the ensuing civil war.

One of the earliest attempts to reach the blast site was initiated in 1921 by Soviet geologist Leonid Kulik, who failed in his first effort, but did eventually make his way to Tunguska six years later. Upon arriving, the devastation caused by the event was unmistakable even after nearly two decades.

Curiously, at the blast site's presumed epicenter, a small area of unaffected trees remained standing, albeit stripped of some of their bark and branches. The surrounding countryside, by comparison, was littered with large numbers of trees that were toppled as the shock waves produced by the exploding asteroid high above radiated downward.

In the decades that followed, additional assessment of the site that included expeditions and aerial surveys, primarily during the 1950s and 1960s, revealed another curious feature: a distinctive hourglass- or butterfly-shaped destruction zone spanning well over 800 square miles (2,070 square kilometers), with millions of trees estimated to have been flattened. Yet most curious of all had been what investigators did not find; despite a blast zone of this size, there was no evidence of an impact crater at Tunguska.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: What the evidence seemed to suggest was that an explosion had occurred not on the surface following a massive impact, but instead high in Earth's atmosphere — probably as much as several miles above the Earth — as tremendous aerodynamic stresses caused the object to fragment and release its energy before reaching the ground.

A longstanding debate about the Tunguska object has centered on whether it was more likely an asteroid or a comet, although today, most evidence appears to favor an asteroid. Among the clues supporting an asteroid origin are mineral and chemical signatures identified in material collected from the region that researchers have argued are consistent with a stony or carbonaceous asteroid. However, identifying physical remnants definitively associated with the Tunguska object has remained challenging.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: While the Tunguska event remains an enigma in some ways, it also offers modern researchers an opportunity to study one of the rare recent examples in Earth's geological history of a large-scale cosmic airburst.

Deeper in Earth's past — around 66 million years ago — a six-mile-wide (10 km) asteroid struck what is now Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula. The impact created the 120-mile-wide (190 km) Chicxulub crater in a cataclysmic event that drove mass extinctions across the planet, eliminating nearly three-quarters of the species that thrived on Earth until that time.

Of course, even objects orders of magnitude smaller than the object that created the Chicxulub crater can pose a danger to Earth. Although the object that struck Earth 66 million years ago is believed to have been as much as 200 times wider and millions of times more massive than the suspected asteroid that exploded over Siberia in 1908, estimates indicate that a Tunguska-scale event would be capable of killing millions if it occurred today over a city the size of New York.

Such estimates aren't based entirely on theory, either. In February 2013, planetary scientists were given a dramatic opportunity to gauge the effects of such an event when a previously undetected 60-foot-wide (20 meters) asteroid exploded after entering Earth's atmosphere over Chelyabinsk, Russia.

The resulting blast, which released energy equivalent to an estimated 500 kilotons of TNT, was captured on cameras throughout the region as it damaged buildings and caused injuries to more than 1,000 people, mostly due to flying glass from windows that were shattered by the blast wave.

Because of events like Chelyabinsk and Tunguska, planetary scientists have worked to expand initiatives that detect and monitor potentially hazardous near-Earth objects (NEOs) that could become a concern in the decades ahead.

Still, despite such efforts having been in effect at the time, the Chelyabinsk event represented an example of a potentially dangerous NEO that effectively managed to sneak up on us. Fortunately, despite the damage that was caused, things could have been far worse. But will we be so lucky next time?

To help mitigate such concerns, in 2016 NASA established the Planetary Defense Coordination Office to help align its efforts with those of its international partners and develop more advanced methods of identifying and tracking any NEOs that could pose an impact threat.

Then in 2022, NASA's Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) demonstrated the use of a spacecraft as a kinetic impactor, which was intentionally sent on a collision course with Dimorphos, the small moon of the asteroid Didymos, which altered Dimorphos' orbital period around its companion by approximately 33 minutes. Such technology could one day prove to be vital if another potential Tunguska-type object were found to be on a collision course with Earth.
Fact, fiction, and planning for the future

Given the questions that remain about Tunguska, as well as the misrepresentations and persistent myths surrounding it, several scientists have also worked in recent years to combat misinformation about the 1908 event.

In a paper published in March 2026 in the journal Meteoritics & Planetary Science, authors Mark Boslough and colleagues noted that future planning for evacuation plans and other mitigation efforts "depend critically on our ability to model these events, which depends on our understanding of the governing physics, which in turn is validated by sparse data on real events such as Tunguska."
"If people do not have confidence in the models on which evacuation plans are based, they could lose their lives," the study's authors warned.

More than a century after it occurred, June 30 is now recognized as International Asteroid Day, commemorating not only the blast's anniversary, but also the need for awareness of the dangerous potential future similar events could present.

Tunguska therefore remains a source of fascination for scientists, as well as an opportunity to better understand — and to prepare for — any potential future threats posed by similar objects, should one eventually be found on a collision course with Earth.

articles.title: How the impossible geometry of 'Tomb Raider III''s UFO level was made
articles.author: Daryl Baxter

paras.en: "Tomb Raider" celebrates its 30th anniversary this month. While many remember the iconic T-Rex or locking Winston the Butler in the freezer, many forget about the UFO in 1998’s "Tomb Raider III"; a mysterious alien craft that worked a lot like Doctor Who’s TARDIS.

Coming off the back of the hugely successful "Tomb Raider 2", developer Core Design had big plans for the third entry, including kayaking, those iconic London levels, and, of course, a level featuring a UFO in Area 51. Although it looked small on the outside, the UFO featured multiple floors for players to explore as they searched for a vital artifact, all as enemies swarmed in.

Now, I'm something of a Tomb Raider historian, and my upcoming book — "The Making of Tomb Raider: 1997-2000" (available from October 30) — goes into detail about the making of "Tomb Raider III", "Tomb Raider IV", and other games in the series during those three years. While writing the book, I spoke to level designer Richard Morton about how the physics-defying UFO was made and how shows like "The X-Files" inspired him and the team.

When you start "Tomb Raider III", you find Lara in India, stumbling across one of four artifacts. After completing India, you can choose between London, South Pacific, and Nevada to collect the other artifacts before reaching the final section in Antarctica.

Richard Morton was one of the designers for "Tomb Raider III", who took on South Pacific and some of Nevada, a location that Neal Boyd had already begun work on before he moved to "Project Eden". Eventually, Lara would find herself in Area 51, with the final part of the level taking place in a UFO that houses the artifact she seeks.

“Area 51 was a bit of a team effort,” reveals Morton. “The part where the rocket launches, Neal did a lot of that stuff. So much of that level is his work, as well as some of the other routes. Andy Sandham helped in finishing off that level, too. And then the bit with the UFO, that was mine.”
Of course, a level called Area 51 needed aliens. In the late 1990s, UFOs were everywhere, ranging from TV shows like The X-Files to countless documentaries on whether aliens were real.

“We knew Area 51 had to have aliens in it in some form. And we did put some down on operating tables – we were all influenced by films and shows like 'The X-Files' and 'Independence Day', which were around at the time of TR3.”

You’d run past the UFO at certain points in between toggling switches, collecting keys, and even launching a rocket. Eventually, you’d unlock a door, letting you in to reveal an impossibly large interior. But all wasn’t as it seemed, and the journey to get here was fraught with challenges.

“I was working quite late one evening, and it wasn't a UFO to start with. I was working on the level and suddenly wondered what would happen if I had three rooms next to each other, with the room in the middle that was only the width of the portal,” explains Morton. “Then I’d link that to a separate room that was only visible inside the portal. I then somehow managed to build this impossible room that was surrounded by eight rooms – the only way I could get it to work. And it did, but it worked horizontally – it was just like Valve's 'Portal', but nine years before.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: AI programmer Tom Scutt, who had joined the team to improve the artificial intelligence for the enemies, worked with Morton to see how a portal could work in the level.

“Tom loved it, but I think he started doing some tests around it – this was just a portal in a room to see if it could be used. Soon after, he explained to me that enemies wouldn't work with it without being heavily reworked, because of how the navigation worked with the enemies,” Morton explains. “So if Lara went through a portal to 'another world', for example, the enemies wouldn't know; they'd just stay in the same room. So all in all, they basically said that they loved it, but you can't do it - and yet I kept trying.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: With Area 51 taking shape and the portal idea becoming viable, Morton realized that the two could become one, resulting in the UFO. “The next night, I decided to build a UFO, which we'd already built within the level in this rough shape in one of the hangars at the end of the level.”

That night, Morton cracked it, meaning the inside of the UFO could now be far bigger. “I built a ladder going up from the entrance, which went straight up through the tiny UFO model, which was only three by three blocks, with a one-block hole going up into it. So I remade the same trick from the night before, only vertically, and it worked!”
Still, despite getting the trick to work, more had to be done to ensure no bugs would emerge during this final section of the level.

“Once you got inside the UFO, I think we had to do a tiny bit of fiddling around, just to make the enemies warp inside the UFO. But they'd only try to attack you when you were in the UFO. I think we triggered them once you got in there and de-triggered them once you came out, just to stop them from firing at you when you weren't in there, just to keep that illusion of this TARDIS UFO going.”

Programmer Martin Gibbins, who had previously warned that the UFO would break everything, was won over by it. “Despite the UFO being Richard's idea, that was a testament to Gavin Rummery's ridiculous portal system. It had a single-block doorway into what was effectively a room. That was the clip window for the rest of the world, so you could do whatever you'd like inside of it. He got it working, and I thought it was great.”

For its time, it was an amazing feat on PlayStation and PC. With this being the third mainline "Tomb Raider" game, some players felt that the series was getting stale. But it was moments like the UFO and discovering it was far bigger than many initially thought that stuck with players, and still does to this day.

Unfortunately, another moment like the UFO would not happen in subsequent games, with the pressure of making the Thanksgiving deadline looming over the team. But Morton reveals that the team did speak about what could have alternatively happened at the end of the level.

"I think we talked about having a portal room that took you to another area that could have been either another location on Earth or another location across the galaxy. But obviously, we just didn't have time to do anything like that. It would have been awesome, though.”
However, after Morton spent two evenings trying to get the UFO to work and some on the team worried that it would break the game, it became a big highlight of "Tomb Raider III".

“When I showed the team the UFO, they were basically trembling, thinking, 'What have you done now!?' And we found out that it did work, and they ended up loving it. Looking back, I couldn't believe that I'd pulled it off, to be honest. I couldn't believe that the engine didn't just crash the game every time the camera looked into that portal. It didn't crash, and I thought, ‘Wow, that's awesome,’ at the time.”

The impossible geometry of the "Tomb Raider III" UFO is indeed an impressive spectacle, even almost 30 years later. If you’re interested in seeing how the TARDIS/UFO works, you can play "Tomb Raider III" via the Remastered collection, available on PlayStation 4/5, Xbox Series, Nintendo Switch 1/2, iOS, Android, and PC via Steam.
If you want to know more about "Tomb Raider 3" and its enigmatic UFO, "The Making of Tomb Raider: 1997-2000" is available from October 30 via Pen and Sword, Amazon, and other retailers.

The Making of Tomb Raider: 1997-2000 tells the untold story of a pivotal period about one of the most successful video game series of all time, as a new development team at Core Design took charge of Tomb Raider in 1997.
Daryl is an entertainment writer and author of two books—The Making of Tomb Raider and 50 Years of Boss Fights.

articles.title: SpaceX launches Falcon 9 Starlink mission for 1st time in more than 3 weeks (photos)
articles.author: Mike Wall

paras.en: SpaceX just broke an uncharacteristically long Starlink launch drought.

The company sent 27 of its Starlink internet satellites to low Earth orbit (LEO) today (Oct. 12), launching them atop a Falcon 9 rocket from California's Vandenberg Space Force Base at 8:28 p.m. EDT (5:28 p.m. local time; 0028 GMT on Oct. 13)

It was the first Starlink mission for a Falcon 9 since Sept. 19, which was another 27-satellite liftoff from Vandenberg. For some perspective on this recent gap: Between Aug. 19 and Sept. 6, a span of 19 days, SpaceX launched seven Starlink missions with Falcon 9s.

SpaceX did loft a batch of Starlinks after that, but it wasn't aboard a Falcon 9. The company's Starship megarocket carried 26 next-gen Starlink V3 craft on its 14th test flight, which took place on Sept. 28.

Starship reached orbit for the first time ever on Flight 14, and it deployed the Starlinks successfully as well. This will happen many more times going forward, if all goes to plan: The Starlink V3 constellation will eventually consist of about 100,000 satellites, all of which will fly on Starship, Elon Musk has said.

Indeed, SpaceX plans to sunset the Falcon 9 and its cousin, the Falcon Heavy, in the next few years, shifting their duties over to the fully reusable, far more powerful Starship, which remains in the test-flight phase.

That shift will be a big one for the spaceflight community, for the Falcon 9 is the workhorse rocket of its generation. In 2025, for example, it flew 165 times — roughly the same number as the rest of the world's orbital launchers combined. Nearly three-quarters of those Falcon 9 launches were Starlink missions.

Things have slowed down a bit in 2026. Today's flight was the 112th Falcon 9 liftoff of the year, and the 82nd in service of the Starlink megaconstellation, which currently consists of more than 11,100 active satellites.

All went according to plan on today's launch. The Falcon 9's first stage came back to Earth as planned, touching down about 8.5 minutes after launch on the drone ship "Of Course I Still Love You," which was stationed in the Pacific Ocean. It was the 20th launch and landing for this particular booster, which is designated B1088.
The rocket's expendable upper stage, meanwhile, delivered the 27 spacecraft to LEO, deploying them there 62 minutes after liftoff, SpaceX announced via X.

Michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. He primarily covers human and robotic spaceflight, military space, and exoplanets, but has been known to dabble in the space art beat. His book about the search for alien life, "Out There," was published on Nov. 13, 2018. Before becoming a science writer, Michael worked as a herpetologist and wildlife biologist. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz. articles.title: India: UN rights office urges release of ‘arbitrarily detained’ protesters

paras.en: India: UN rights office urges release of ‘arbitrarily detained’ protesters

The UN human rights office (OHCHR) has voiced concern over reports of mass detentions in India of demonstrators, protest leaders, civil society members, lawyers and journalists, before and during large-scale protests in Delhi on Saturday.

The demonstration was called by a youth-led movement that is seeking electoral reforms ahead of state elections, with its chief demand being the resignation of the official heading India’s election commission.
Protesters have criticised the body’s revision of the national voter roll, which has reportedly removed tens of millions of names in a bid to avoid duplicates and discrepancies.
Political opponents argue it is an exercise to keep the ruling nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) in power.
Police refused permission for Saturday’s protest to take place at the movement’s planned venue in the capital, and heavy security and road closures were reported.
Media reports say the movement’s leaders were among those detained.
UN human rights office spokesperson Thameen Al-Kheetan called on the authorities to ensure that the right to peaceful assembly is “fully respected and fulfilled”.
“Restrictions on peaceful protests must meet strict tests of necessity and proportionality,” he said.
He urged law enforcement officers to show “utmost restraint” in responding to peaceful protesters, in keeping with India’s democratic traditions and its human rights obligations.
Mr. Al-Kheetan said that anyone arbitrarily detained must be released immediately and unconditionally.
He also encouraged the authorities to engage in meaningful dialogue to address what he described as broadly held concerns.

articles.title: Giving a dam: Cultivating peace in Côte d’Ivoire

paras.en: Giving a dam: Cultivating peace in Côte d’Ivoire

Adam Ouattara and Makongo Traoré have four children and a home on the edge of Torla village in Côte d’Ivoire. He herds cattle. She grows vegetables on a small plot nearby. For years, the dry season pitted their two livelihoods against each other.
As grazing land and water points dried up, Mr. Ouattara and other herders have had to push their cattle farther from the village, often straight through cultivated fields.

Damaged crops led to disputes with farmers, a familiar dry-season strain across much of northern Côte d’Ivoire, where seasonal pastoral movement and expanding farmland increasingly compete for the same ground.

“When resources become scarce, everyone is trying to protect their livelihood,” said Mr. Ouattara, who has led the local herders association since 2021, representing pastoralists in disputes and community talks.
A rehabilitated agropastoral dam, completed this August, is changing that math. The dam now holds more water and releases it more reliably through the dry months, for livestock and irrigation alike.
For Mr. Ouattara, the shift shows up in fewer confrontations. “Today, we sit together and discuss,” he said. “There are fewer conflicts.”
For Ms. Traoré, it shows up in her fields. A steady water supply has let her expand her vegetable plot – work she says now supports her children’s schooling. The maths is easy.
“If we can work well in our fields,” she said, “we can provide for our children and send them to school. Before, the lack of water made life difficult.”

In a region where many herders move seasonally with their livestock, access to water plays a critical role in supporting livelihoods and fostering social cohesion between pastoralist and agricultural communities.

The dam is already helping create conditions for peaceful co-existence between herders and farmers in Torla, managed locally by the community and supported by the International Organization for Migration (IOM), the UN Peacebuilding Fund and partners.
The goal is simple: Prevent conflicts linked to competition over natural resources and boost community resilience.
The results are already playing out in Torla, where a new chapter of community dialogue and shared resource management has begun.
For residents, this project goes beyond livestock or agriculture, representing an opportunity to build a more resilient future.
“The dam brings peace to the village,” Mr. Ouattara said. “Today, we can access water here and that reduces many of the challenges we faced before.”

For Ms. Traoré, reliable access to water means greater stability for her vegetable plot and her family. It also means new opportunities for women in the community for market gardening, an important source of household income in the area.
“Now, we have the possibility to work harder and ensure a better future for our children,” she said.
Like many communities across northern Côte d’Ivoire, Torla has witnessed changing environmental conditions in recent years.

According to Adam Ouattara, increasing pressure on land has affected traditional grazing patterns: during the rainy season, agricultural production expands, leaving less space available for livestock.
“When the cultivators grow crops, much of the land is occupied, and our animals have to move farther away, sometimes towards the borders, to find pasture,” he explained.

Such challenges highlight the importance of investments that support both farming and pastoral activities while promoting peaceful co-existence. As president of the herders' association, Mr. Outtara has witnessed significant progress through improved dialogue.
“Today, we sit together and discuss,” he said. “We approach one another to talk and understand each other. There are fewer conflicts.”

articles.title: Sudan: Drought and war push Darfur and Kordofan towards famine

paras.en: Sudan: Drought and war push Darfur and Kordofan towards famine

The risk of famine is growing in parts of Sudan already torn apart by war, as a severe El Niño drought makes life even harder in Greater Darfur and Greater Kordofan, the UN-backed global hunger monitor warned on Monday.

In a new alert, the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) said fresh evidence shows malnutrition getting worse in several hotspots. Aid is not keeping up, held back by a severe lack of funding, insecurity and restricted access.
The IPC food insecurity alert index is a global partnership that includes the UN emergency food agency WFP and the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO).

In Eastern Jebel Marra, South Darfur, a survey of two camps for displaced people found acute malnutrition among children at 38 and 30.8 per cent – above the threshold for famine. Hunger was severe and death rates were high.
Across Greater Darfur, 13 of the 17 nutrition surveys carried out since January found critical levels of acute malnutrition.
In Nyala, the share of children seeking nutrition help who needed treatment for severe acute malnutrition more than doubled between January and August, from five to 11 per cent.
Drought now covers more than half of Sudan, wiping out crops in some areas and leaving families without food or income.
In North Darfur, 64 per cent of cropland is showing poor plant growth.
Rains arrived in late September, too late to save most cereal crops, the alert said, and cereal prices are very likely to keep rising.

Greater Kordofan, described in the alert as the epicentre of Sudan’s conflict, has seen more than 300,000 people forced from their homes since October 2025. Markets have been hit by more than 170 airstrikes, looting incidents or armed clashes this year.
Aid workers face extreme danger. Two trucks contracted by WFP came under fire on 2 and 3 October, killing at least one person.

Children are going without treatment. As of August, only 26 per cent of those expected to need care for severe acute malnutrition with medical complications had received it. Without treatment, as many as two thirds of them could die.
As of 8 October, less than half of the humanitarian appeal for Sudan had been funded.
The IPC’s Famine Review Committee said there is not enough survey data for a full analysis, but the evidence points to a rapidly worsening situation.
“Famine is the collapse of systems,” the committee said. “We are witnessing a humanitarian catastrophe, already of historic proportions.”

The alert called for an end to the fighting, safe and sustained access for aid agencies – especially in North and West Kordofan – and flexible funding on a large scale. Without a major increase in help, it warned, more lives will be at risk.

articles.title: Renshaw stars as Australia close in on first Test victory in Durban

paras.en: South Africa vs Australia: Matt Renshaw stars as tourists close in on first Test victory in Durban

Matt Renshaw followed his first-innings 190 with 82 before taking his maiden Test wicket; Australia declared with a lead of 420 and South Africa closed on 102-4; watch day five of the first Test live on Sky Sports Cricket on Tuesday, with coverage starting from 8am
Matt Renshaw continued to hog centre stage as Australia pushed closer to winning the first Test against South Africa in Durban.

Renshaw added a second-innings knock of 82 to his game-shaping 190 and was not finished there. After Australia declared with a lead of 420, the occasional off-spinner picked up his maiden Test wicket as the Proteas laboured to 102-4.

South Africa captain Temba Bavuma was his victim, caught off bat and pad by Nic Maddinson for just one. Josh Hazlewood had already got the ball rolling, dismissing Ryan Rickelton and David Bedingham, with Pat Cummins adding Tristan Stubbs before the close on day four.
- Scorecard: South Africa vs Australia – first Test
- Get the latest Sky Sports deals or stream with no contract

Aiden Markram will resume on 45 not out alongside Wiaan Mulder but the odds are stacked against the hosts salvaging the game on day five. Australia were without Steve Smith's brilliance at slip after he was hit on the helmet by Anrich Nortje and was subsequently replaced in the field pending further assessments.
Renshaw's second innings bore almost no relation to his first. The 190 came at a strike-rate of 47. The 82 came at 82, with seven fours and two sixes in it.
Then it took a freak moment to end it. The ball went through Keshav Maharaj's hands more than once and off his own head before it stayed put, by which time the bowler was flat on the pitch.
Renshaw was on for twin centuries when it happened. Instead he finished with 272 runs for the match, which is close to the most any Australian has made against South Africa.

Three more runs would have put him level with Phillip Hughes, who made twin tons on this ground in 2009. Nine more and he would have passed David Warner's pair of centuries in Cape Town in 2014. Bradman's 299 not out was 28 away.
Nobody else in the Australian order got past 48. Maddinson stopped there, Marnus Labuschagne on 37, Smith on 27 and Alex Carey on 24.
Captain Cummins hurries things along for Australia
Australia resumed on 33-0 and never looked like batting for time. They were 174-4 at lunch and 280 in front, with Maddinson's 48 from 38 balls setting the rate.

Labuschagne then produced the day's statistical curiosity. He made 37 from 58 balls, exactly what he managed in the first innings, which is only the 12th known instance of a batter matching his runs and his balls faced in both innings of a men's Test.
But Smith's 27 was the innings Nortje will remember. The bouncer that hit him on the helmet arrived on the fourth ball he faced and Smith answered by taking 14 off one Nortje over.
Cricket Australia said he was being assessed for concussion and he will be monitored for 24 hours.
Cummins made the rest a formality. His 32 not out took just a dozen balls, with Simon Harmer conceding three of his four sixes inside one over. The declaration came shortly before tea on 314-6.
Markram the last line of resistance for hosts
South Africa were left 421 to win, which no side in Test history has managed.
West Indies' 418 against Australia in Antigua in 2003 is still the mark and the best at this ground is 336, chased by Australia in 1950.
Batting out the day is the realistic hope and the record there is thin. Just two sides in the last 13 years have lasted 140 overs to save a Test.
Rickelton pulled at a short one in the fourth over and Carey took the catch, two runs made with Hazlewood again the bowler who had him.
Markram and Bedingham put on 66 in 19.4 overs before Hazlewood pinned Bedingham in front for 46. He was 49 first time round, so twice in the match he got into the forties and no further.
Three wickets went down for 13 runs from there and South Africa were 86-4, scoring across the innings at 2.48 an over.
Markram has needed 115 balls for his 45 not out and he was dropped on the way, on 15, when the chance hit Carey on the elbow and ran away past slip.

Among players still active, only Kusal Mendis of Sri Lanka averages more than Markram's 45.56 in a fourth innings. His 136 won the World Test Championship final against these same opponents at Lord's.
He has been in this position at this ground before, too. He made 143 here in 2018 chasing 417 against Australia, 340 minutes of work that still ended in defeat.
He will be hoping that something miraculous can happen on Tuesday with Australia needing six wickets to win and South Africa still requiring 319 runs.

articles.title: Suljovic apologises but faces probe over inciting jeers and alleged sexist comments

paras.en: Mensur Suljovic referred to darts regulator for inciting jeers against Ross Smith and alleged sexist comments as Austrian issues apology

Mensur Suljovic has been referred to the Darts Regulation Authority for his incitement of jeers against Ross Smith in their clash at the Swiss Darts Trophy; he has also been referred over his alleged sexist comments in an interview about the incident; the Austrian has issued an apology

Mensur Suljovic's crowd incitement during his match against Ross Smith and his alleged sexist comments in his on-stage interview regarding the incident have been referred to the Darts Regulation Authority.
The Austrian encouraged the crowd to boo the Englishman during a last-leg decider in their third-round clash at the Swiss Darts Trophy on Sunday afternoon.
He was later asked about the incident in an on-stage interview and used an allegedly sexist comment to describe how Smith reacted.
- Smith vows 'karma' will catch up with Suljovic

- Not got Sky? Get instant access with NOW 📺
Suljovic said: "Ross Smith is one of the best players in the world - what's the bloke complaining about? He's got to play his game; otherwise, he's welcome to go home.
"Women, women - they're always complaining, sorry. Sorry, you don't do that. I fully accept him as one of the very best darts players.
"OK, I've been riling up the crowd a bit, just like in Germany - I need your support. I need you; without you, I can't achieve anything. Thank you, thank you very much!
"What's he complaining about? When I'm in England, everyone's against me; everywhere I go.
"And now, all of a sudden, he's complaining? He might as well just stay at home."
On Monday afternoon, Suljovic subsequently issued an apology.
"I would like to comment once again on my match against Ross Smith and the interview that followed," he said.
"The emotions got the better of me in that moment. I wanted to get the crowd behind me and, in doing so, I didn't properly realise that Ross was throwing for the match.
"Looking back, I understand that the timing was unfortunate and was perceived as unfair. I would like to apologise to Ross for that.
"Ross is, in my opinion, one of the best darts players in the world, and I have great respect for him and his achievements.
"My comment about women during the interview was also completely inappropriate. I should never have said something like that. I would like to sincerely apologise to all women for those remarks.
"Darts thrives on emotion, but fairness and respect are just as important. Yesterday, I let my emotions get the better of me.
In a statement, the PDC confirmed "the matter on stage and interview has now been referred to the Darts Regulation Authority" and issued "no further comment".
The incident between Suljovic and Smith explained

Suljovic and Smith were locked at 5-5 in their best-of-11-legs clash on Sunday afternoon, with Smith having two match darts at double 18 when Suljovic gestured to the crowd to increase the volume of boos, prompting the Englishman to miss the target and hand his opponent a chance to steal the match.
Suljovic then nailed double 10 with his final dart to complete the checkout and seal victory.
His antics had left Smith frustrated, with the Englishman later taking to X to share his thoughts following the defeat.
"I don't blame Mensur for me losing that game," Smith wrote. "I missed two match darts. Simple as that.
"Obviously, it's impossible for me to know what he's doing behind my back when I'm throwing apart from the crowd's response.
Suljovic is no stranger to controversial incidents. The Austrian denied intentionally provoking Joe Cullen during a World Championship clash last December.

Cullen branded his opponent's pace of play as "cheating" and "not darts" after becoming frustrated by the length of time he was taking to retrieve his darts and celebrate, with referee Kirk Bevans even forced to intervene.
Webster: There is a time and place for it and it was 'poor form'
Sky Sports Darts' Mark Webster on the incident between Smith and Suljovic (speaking before the apology)...
"Obviously with regards to the weekend, it was poor form for Mensur Suljovic.
"I think every player can use the crowd to their advantage, but there's a time to do it, isn't there?
"It's not while the player's throwing, particularly not on match darts.
"Fair play to Ross, he came out and said he didn't even see it and it didn't put him off, he still should have won the game.
"Mensur kind of doubled down on it as well. Like I said, get the crowd involved, players do it, it's part of the game now, but not on match darts and geeing them up when he's on match darts.
"He has used tactics in the past, hasn't he, in terms of slowing players down.
"That's fine, it's not against the rules, but sort of egging on the crowd when Ross on match darts wasn't good.
"I'm sure the DRA will get involved now, it's not good sportsmanship, is it? Rightly so, he should get fined.
"As long as he recognises that he's done wrong, he hasn't at the minute, but when he recognises that he's done wrong, it's the timing of it, isn't it, that's the poorest.
"I'm sure he'll realise and a fine will come his way. He should learn from it and he should never do it again, not on match darts."
